extracted.intended_audience: analytical chemists and scientific researchers (readers of Royal Society papers)
extracted.subtask_description: Laboratory reports and methodological guidance for quantitative analytical chemistry experiments and observations (e.g., water purification analyses and salt composition determinations). Emphasizes purification of reagents, experimental controls, multiple analytic routes, and careful weighing/conditioning of materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record temporal physical changes of samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe and document changes in appearance, odour, and sedimentation over time (e.g., clarity improving over weeks; formation of scum and surface stratum; separation into flakes with attached air bubbles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author documents that water 'become much clearer' over several weeks, a scum formed a 'pretty regular stratum about half an inch in thickness', and that masses separated into flakes with 'minute air bubbles' imparting buoyancy. Report time intervals and qualitative changes (clarity, odour, sediment behaviour) to characterise spontaneous processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the same analytical method for comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject new samples to the same mode of analysis previously employed to permit direct comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After depuration the water 'was filtered through paper, and was then subjected to the same mode of analysis which was employed on the former occasion'. Always repeat prior analytic protocols when comparing results across specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify residues and report per standard mass
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the mass of evaporative residue using a standard basis (e.g., grains per 10,000 grains of water) so results are comparable and interpretable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '10,000 grains left by evaporation a saline crust ... which ... weighed 7-0 grains.' Convert to conventional units and relate to thresholds (e.g., grains per pint) where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify ionic/salt composition and state assumed combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting quantities of acids/bases/oxides, state the assumed chemical combinations (e.g., sulphuric acid combined with lime; muriatic acid combined with magnesia or soda) used to compute respective salt quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes, 'If we suppose the sulphuric acid to be combined with a part of the lime, and the remainder of the lime to be in the state of carbonate...' and then gives respective quantities. Explicitly declare such stoichiometric assumptions used in converting analytic tests into salt amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess effects of purification on mineral content and hardness
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine whether depuration or other treatments remove organics but concentrate saline/earthy matters (hardness), and discuss suitability of treated water for intended uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper warns that depuration 'freed itself from the great quantity of organic matter ... yet the quantity of saline matter is increased as much as four-fold.' Relate measured saline content to practical thresholds (e.g., 'water which contains as much as 5 grains in the pint ... regarded as too hard').

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider mechanism (e.g., fermentation) linking observations to products
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret observed changes mechanistically (e.g., depuration as a species of fermentation producing gaseous products while leaving salts in solution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author frames the depurating process as 'a species of fermentation' producing gaseous compounds and leaving saline bodies behind. Use observed gas evolution, changes in odour, and residue composition to support mechanistic classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test multiple reagents/procedures for colour and impurity removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Try different treatments (boiling, sand & charcoal filtration, alum, metallic salts such as sulphate of iron) and report which are effective for removing colouring/extractive matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'this colouring matter was not removed by boiling, nor by filtration through sand and charcoal, but that alum and certain metallic salts ... threw down a precipitate, and left the water without colour.' Report conditions (heated, proportions) and relative effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterize sediment qualitatively and weigh after standardized drying
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the heterogeneous components of sediment (siliceous sand, organic fibres, coal fragments, sulfides, etc.) and report mass after drying at a specified temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sediment 'consisted of all those substances casually introduced into the Thames'; when 'completely dried at a temperature of 200°' it weighed about a given proportion. Provide qualitative description plus standardized drying/temperature conditions for quantitative reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize sample heterogeneity and avoid over-detail where unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that composition varies across samples/locations; avoid attempting minute examination when variability makes it unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author states the mass 'must of course differ, both in quantity and in quality, in every different portion of the water, so to render it unnecessary to attempt a more minute examination of them.' Note when broader characterisation suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize prior literature and repeated foundational measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: Review and attempt to reproduce foundational experiments/analyses (e.g., determinations used to infer atomic weights), because errors in such experiments propagate widely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner re-examines Dr. Thomson's use of chloride of barium to determine equivalents, observing discordant results reported by others (Berzelius) and stressing the need to 'review our stock of information' and 'ascertaining with the greatest possible care the exact ratio' of elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purify reagents thoroughly and document purification steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare and purify reagents (salts, acids, silver, etc.) by repeated crystallization, distillation, fusing, alcohol washing, redissolution, and other means; document these steps to justify accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sulphuric acid 'purified by distillation', sulphate of potash 'prepared by repeated crystallization', chloride of barium fused and boiled in alcohol and redissolved in distilled water. Describe each purification and why it was done.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove trace contaminants (e.g., iron, manganese) before analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat solutions (e.g., render alkaline) to precipitate possible contaminants such as iron or manganese before crystallising the analyte.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chloride of barium solution 'was rendered alkaline with pure baryta, in order to precipitate any oxide of iron or manganese which might be present.' Include such pretreatments to avoid interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for hygroscopic behavior and weigh salts under controlled conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: When working with hygroscopic/anomalous salts (e.g., anhydrous chloride of barium that 'attracts moisture freely'), weigh in sealed containers and take precautions (weigh when cold after placing hot in a weighed bottle with tight cork).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasises placing hot chloride in a weighed bottle secured by a tight cork and weighing when cold. State hygroscopic handling procedures and their rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use orthogonal methods to cross-check composition (double-route analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine composition by at least two independent chemical routes (e.g., precipitate baryta with sulphuric acid and determine chlorine by precipitating with nitrate of silver) to validate results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner's two-part process: precipitate baryta as sulphate and independently precipitate chloride as silver chloride; compare both results to detect method-specific errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate and correct for adherence/occlusion of one salt on another
rubrics_metrics.description: Be alert that one reagent (e.g., sulphate of potash) may tenaciously adhere to an insoluble precipitate (e.g., sulphate of baryta), biasing weight; examine adhesion under different conditions and quantify its effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner documents that 'a small portion of the latter invariably escapes decomposition, and falls tenaciously adhering to the sulphate of baryta' and quantifies the effect (up to ~1% weight). Vary mixing, temperature, concentration, and washing to study the phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary experimental conditions to test robustness (temperature, concentration, ratios)
rubrics_metrics.description: Test how changes in mixing temperature, solution strength, relative quantities, presence of other salts, and extent/manner of washing affect outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner varied experiments by mixing at boiling temperature, continuing ebullition, edulcoration with boiling water, and noting results remained the same. Report how parameter changes affect completeness of reactions and residual impurities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wash precipitates until washings show no trace of the analyte
rubrics_metrics.description: Edulcorate (wash) the precipitate repeatedly until washings cease to contain the precipitated ion, and document the washing medium and whether acidulated or boiling water was used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The precipitate was 'edulcorated until the washings ceased to contain a trace of baryta.' But Turner also notes some adherent salts remain despite extensive washing; document the washing protocol and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dry/ignite precipitates to constant weight under specified conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Dry or ignite precipitates (e.g., sulphate of baryta 'dried by exposure to a red heat') to constant weight before weighing and state the heating conditions used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give temperatures/conditions (red heat, drying at 200° for sediment) and note possible differences between methods (evaporation to dryness in capsule vs. collection on filter) and their effect on measured mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer and report measurements from the least manipulation-prone runs
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess which individual experiments are less influenced by handling errors and adopt their mean (or state why a subset mean is chosen) rather than a simple mean of all runs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner found the last two silver-precipitation analyses 'less influenced by errors of manipulation' and therefore adopted their mean instead of the mean of all five. Explain selection of representative data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibrate standards (e.g., hornsilver) and be aware of method biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the composition of standard compounds by repeated experiments and note method-dependent biases (e.g., precipitation by free acid may dissolve some chloride and lower measured yield).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple experiments gave 100 parts silver correspond to ~132.83 parts chloride of silver; Turner notes that precipitation by free muriatic acid yields consistently lower results 'owing to a trace of the chloride being dissolved by the strong acid solution.' Report such biases and their magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform solubility and chemical tests to confirm purity of precipitates
rubrics_metrics.description: After precipitation and washing, test the solid and washings for the presence of analyte or other ions by solubility (e.g., dissolves in ammonia) and by adding acids to check for turbidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner tested silver-precipitated chloride: it 'dissolved completely in ammonia, and the addition of sulphuric acid did not cause the slightest turbidity.' Use such checks to confirm absence of occluded species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for propagation of analytic error into theoretical conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that inaccuracies in common analytic methods (e.g., analyses of sulphate of potash) can mislead determinations of equivalents/atomic weights; treat such numbers with caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner warns that Dr. Thomson's method 'is radically defective' and that many analyses 'must be regarded with suspicion,' noting the downstream impact on equivalent numbers and theoretical claims. Discuss confidence and possible propagation of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report and discuss disagreements with other authoritative results
rubrics_metrics.description: When results differ from other eminent chemists (e.g., Thomson, Berzelius), present detailed procedural differences and reasoned arguments for why results differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner contrasts his sulphate yields with Thomson's and Berzelius's numbers and details procedural differences (possible impure commercial salts, adhesion issues). Provide full experimental detail enabling readers to evaluate sources of discrepancy.
